value.why: The idea is a weekend and the shipped thing is not. Reaching this state means Flutter on two platforms, on-device speech recognition with a typed fallback, an emotion-label pass with day titles and a weekly letter, Firestore plus Firebase Auth/Analytics/Crashlytics, a Cloud Run service, a physics toy in the feelings box, and a RevenueCat entitlement loop with three in-flow gates, a trial and cross-reinstall entitlement correctness - then eight localisations. For one developer that is weeks of integration, most of it on the billing path and the speech path, neither of which the page shows any evidence of testing.

data_and_models.value: User voice recordings (kept on device; only the transcript leaves for the reading), plus typed entries. For VIP, 'coarse voice-level signals' compared to the user's own baseline - the only derived audio feature the page says is sent anywhere, and the page does not say where the baseline is computed. Six fixed emotion labels (joy, bashfulness, surprise, sadness, anger, tiredness), a generated day title and a companion line from Gemini via Vertex AI; a weekly letter from the same model over the week's entries. Firestore holds entries, Firebase Auth identity, Analytics and Crashlytics instrument the funnel, RevenueCat holds entitlement state. No labelled corpus, fine-tune or evaluation set is described, and no retention or usage figure is published.

how_it_works.value: Flutter front end (Android and iOS) with sensors_plus driving the physics in the feelings box, on-device speech recognition through the Apple Speech framework, and Gemini through Vertex AI for the reading and the weekly letter. Firebase Auth, Analytics and Crashlytics plus Firestore for storage, Google Cloud Run behind it. Monetisation is RevenueCat end to end - `purchases_flutter` for products, purchases and entitlements - offered weekly, monthly and yearly with a 7-day free trial. The billing surface is deliberately quiet: feature screens carry no locks and no 'you have run out' dialogs, only a small crown on the longer look-back ranges, and the paywall appears at exactly three in-flow moments - talking a second time in a day, tapping 1mo/3mo/1y, tapping an empty calendar day. Shipped in 8 languages: English, Japanese, Korean, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Traditional Chinese.

how_they_tested.value: Nothing is published about how the reading was validated: no accuracy figure, no labelled set, no comparison against the 1-5 scale it replaces, no agreement between the on-device transcript and a reference transcript, and no retention data for a product whose pitch is that people abandon journaling. The only evidence offered for the design decisions is observational - that early subscribers returned on later days and looked back before paying - stated without counts. No repository, test harness or CI link appears anywhere on the page.

limits_they_disclosed.value: The engineering difficulty the page spends its time on is not the model but the moment of the ask. Placing a paywall in an app whose whole promise is being a place you can put an unspoken feeling without being judged is the tension the design keeps circling, and the answer given is behavioural: 'our first subscribers came back on later days and looked back before paying, so this is where we put the value' - so the value is sold at the look-back and at the missed day, words are always kept first, and declining the prompt loses nothing. The second difficulty is on the other side of the same coin: the mechanics that make a journaling app sticky (streaks, totals, encouragements) are the ones that make it hurt on a bad week, which is why the streak is shown only while it lasts. No implementation obstacle, cost or failure is described.

value.relation: same contract, opposite evidence culture. Both track a person against their own baseline, both refuse to diagnose, both flag unusual change rather than score it. Neuroguard runs timed cognitive and camera-based physical tests with per-test scoring; Kimocchi reads free prose and publishes no figure for how often it reads correctly. The pair is the argument that the soft-input version needs the measurement discipline the clinical version already has, and does not have it.

the same removal of capability-as-a-precondition: medvoice takes reading out of the loop for patients who cannot manage it, Kimocchi takes articulate writing out of the loop for people who cannot manage that at 11pm. Both arrive at 'the interface should not require the thing the user is short of' from opposite directions - clinical necessity and consumer retention.

useful as a contrast in disclosure only: both records state what they will not do, but ZeroDay's limit is an engineering constraint it could not fully solve (retry loops) while Kimocchi's are product boundaries chosen deliberately - a reminder that 'what it deliberately does not do' is a stronger signal than a capability list.

value: The reading, silently. On-device speech recognition on a late-night mumble, then a six-label pass over two minutes of prose: sarcasm, a flat 'I'm fine', a day that was actually bad but got narrated cheerfully all produce a confident label with no uncertainty attached, and the calendar of faces becomes a record of what the model guessed. Because nothing in the UI can tell a wrong label from an unusual day, the failure mode is invisible to exactly the user the product is for.

The VIP voice-level signal is the one place audio-derived features leave the device, and the page does not say whether the baseline it is compared against is computed on device or on the server. If it is server-side, the 'recordings stay on your phone' sentence needs a qualifier a reader can find - for a product whose pitch is privacy, an ambiguous data boundary is a product bug.

The Sunday letter is the second thing to decay: a generated recap of six labels and a handful of day-titles reads warmly for two weeks and templated by week four, and there is no evaluation or user feedback anywhere on the page about whether anyone keeps opening it.

RevenueCat entitlements are the boring break: the trial, the three gates and the crown all depend on entitlement state being correct across reinstall and store-side refunds, and a gate that misfires in a journal the user cannot re-read is worse than a paywall. There is no test or CI evidence for the billing path, which is the path that carries money.

what_it_does.value: Tap the mic and talk for up to two minutes, or type on days you cannot speak out loud. On-device speech recognition turns the audio into text; the model returns six feeling labels (joy, bashfulness, surprise, sadness, anger, tiredness), a short title for the day and one gentle line from the companion. Those labels become physical objects: little characters, one colour per feeling, that drop into that day's box, roll when you tilt the phone, squish when tapped, and fall back in when flung off the screen. A calendar of faces holds every day's words, feelings and your own voice if you kept it, with look-backs over a week, a month or a year, and every Sunday night the companion writes a letter about the week. Four limits are authored as a section of their own: no diagnosis, no advice, no pushy encouragement - 'the AI is instructed to receive, not to fix'; no streak guilt, since a current streak shows only while it lasts, '0 days' and 'streak lost' are never displayed and totals only go up; not a medical device, stated in the app, the store listing and the terms, with signposting to professional help when things feel heavy; and recordings stay on the phone, with only the transcript sent for the reading plus, for VIP, coarse voice-level signals compared against the user's own baseline, and AI can be switched off entirely.

what_it_is.value: Voice journaling that reads six feelings instead of asking for a score: recordings stay on the phone, the model is instructed to receive rather than fix, and the paywall only appears at the moment someone reaches for more.

value: Put the paywall at the moment of reaching and nowhere else: three named triggers, each reached by someone already asking for more, each keeping what they made before the prompt appears (talk twice in a day and your words are stored first; tap 1mo/3mo/1y and you see the week you can already see; tap an empty day and you are invited to fill it). Feature screens carry no locks and no 'you have run out' state at all, only a small crown on the ranges beyond the free window. This is a monetisation rule that costs nothing to adopt and is the opposite of the metered-gate default.

Design the retention mechanic so it cannot punish: a streak is shown only while it is alive, '0 days' and 'streak lost' never render, and totals only go up. In any product where the tracked object is a bad week, the counter is the harm.

State the model's job as a boundary in the product, not in a blog post: 'the AI is instructed to receive, not to fix', no advice, no diagnosis, and the non-medical-device claim made in the app, the store listing and the terms together, with signposting to professional help - plus a switch to turn the AI off entirely, which is the disclosure that makes the rest believable.

Make the derived signal tactile instead of charted: emotions become objects in a box you can tilt, tap and fling. A chart invites analysis; a physics toy invites return. Same data, different second use.

kimocchi-voice-mood-tracker.worth_note: What is on this page is craft at a level the rest of the corpus does not reach - a shipped, monetised, eight-language app with the entitlement loop wired end to end - but craft is not evidence of an idea worth building over. The shape itself is already in the corpus twice: neuroguard-ai scores short tests against the patient's own baseline and flags change without diagnosing, medvoice removes reading from the loop for people who cannot do it; Kimocchi is the consumer, self-directed version of the same contract. And the load-bearing capability - that a model can read six feelings out of two muttered minutes - is asserted with no accuracy figure, no labelled set and no comparison against the 1-5 scale it claims to replace, so the record that is best evidenced on execution is unevidenced exactly where it needs to be. `niche`, not `strong`: the stealable part is a pattern, not a product.
